name: Quilt Cruise
character: Classrooms at sea: itinerary-led, teacher-forward, and packing-list practical for quilting cruises and retreats away from home.

sections.eyebrow: Quilting cruises, charter sails, and one very patient riverboat
sections.title: Classrooms at sea

items.title: The classroom
items.body: A dedicated conference room converted for sewing: machines, irons, cutting stations, and a design wall that has survived eleven storms.

items.title: Classes

items.title: Ports
items.body: A morning ashore between every two sewing days, with fabric shop intel gathered the honest way.

sections.heading: The classroom, in practice
sections.html:
Leave your machine at home. The classroom holds twenty-four set up machines that stay standing all week, so mid-voyage you sew exactly where you left off instead of at a folding table wedged between dinner seats.

Sewing days run 9 to 5 with the buffet two decks up. Sea days are for the top; port mornings are for the ship's photographer and the local quilt shop, if the port has one, which we have checked.

items.quote: I finished the top, watched whales from the design wall, and did not carry a machine onto a single airplane.
items.author: P., 2025 Alaska sailing

items.quote: My husband fished. I sewed. We met for dinner and both had stories.
items.author: D., Caribbean voyage

sections.heading: How booking works
sections.html: A deposit holds the cabin and the classroom seat. Final payment follows the cruise line's schedule, and transfers to another sailing are free up to ninety days out. Cabins are held for solo quilters willing to share, matched by the office with more success than luck.

sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Teachers who pack their own seam rippers and have never once lost a class to seasickness.

items.title: Foundation paper piecing

items.title: Color and stash

items.body: One block a night, group-assembled on the last sea day, auctioned for the crew welfare fund.

items.quote: Twenty-four students, six days, and not one unfinished kit went home. That has never happened in a hotel ballroom.

sections.heading: How the office runs
sections.html:
We are a licensed travel agency that books only groups it can sit with at dinner. The cabin contracts, the classroom freight, the teachers' airfare, and the machine maintenance contract all live in one binder that has survived every sailing so far.

The rule we steer by: nobody sews alone, nobody carries a machine, and nobody misses the ship because a fabric shop was two blocks past the meeting point. That last one now has a fifteen-minute buffer built into every port plan.

items.quote: They moved fourteen people and two sewing machines across a port strike without one of us opening the cruise line app.
items.author: A group organizer, Miami

sections.title: Reserve a cabin
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Tell us the voyage, your cabin preference, and whether anyone is traveling with you and their sewing intentions.

items.a: Closed-loop sailings accept a birth certificate and photo ID, but we recommend the passport; the one time a year it matters, it really matters.
A fifth of every voyage is here for the buffet and the excursions. There is a shore plan for partners and a standing table at dinner.
The classroom sits mid-ship on a low deck, the stabilizers do most of the work, and the office mails ginger chews with your documents. Bring what your doctor recommends.
Yes: a small number of single cabins, and a share program matched by the office with better results than chance.
